nodes.label: Erode Cloth Market
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: One of the largest cloth markets in the world, located in Tamil Nadu. A bi-weekly market where cloth made by weavers in surrounding villages is sold. Cloth merchants buy here and supply to garment manufacturers and exporters across the country.

nodes.label: Putting-Out System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: An arrangement where merchants supply raw materials (yarn) to weavers and receive finished cloth. Weavers work from home on looms but have no say in pricing or who the final buyer is. Merchants control both raw material supply and market access, giving them significant power over weavers.

nodes.label: Weavers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Weavers and their families work up to 12 hours a day on looms to produce cloth, earning about Rs 3500 per month. Each loom costs Rs 20000. They depend on merchants for yarn supply and selling cloth. They have no knowledge of final selling price or buyer identity.

nodes.label: Weavers Cooperative
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Cooperatives where weavers form a group and collectively procure yarn and do marketing, reducing dependence on merchants. The government helps by buying cloth at reasonable prices. Tamil Nadu runs a Free School Uniform programme procuring from powerloom cooperatives. Co-optex stores sell handloom cooperative cloth.

nodes.label: Garment Exporting Factory
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Factories near Delhi that make shirts from cloth for export to foreign buyers. The Impex factory has 70 workers, mostly women on temporary basis. Workers earn Rs 1500 to Rs 3000 per month. Factories try to maximise profit by getting maximum work at lowest wages.

nodes.label: Foreign Buyer
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Businesspersons from the US and Europe who run chains of stores. They demand lowest prices, set high quality standards, and require timely delivery. A shirt bought from exporter at Rs 200 is sold at Rs 1200 (USD 26) in the US after adding Rs 300 advertising and Rs 100 storage costs, yielding Rs 600 profit.

nodes.label: Market Inequality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Not everyone gains equally in the market. Foreign businesspersons make huge profits, garment exporters moderate profits, while cotton farmers, weavers, and factory workers barely survive. Democracy requires fair wages but market structures create deep inequalities in earnings.

nodes.label: Exploitation of Workers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Garment factory workers, mostly women, work on temporary contracts with low wages. Tailors earn Rs 3000 per month, thread cutters and buttoners Rs 1500. Workers can be dismissed anytime. Women are employed as low-paid helpers. Long hours and job insecurity characterise their conditions.

nodes.label: Debt Trap of Farmers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Small farmers borrow from traders at high interest for seeds, fertilisers, and pesticides. They are then forced to sell produce to the same trader at low prices. The trader deducts loan repayment from payment, leaving farmers with barely enough to survive until the next cycle of borrowing.

nodes.label: Cooperative Model
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: When people with common interests come together to work for mutual benefit. In weavers cooperatives, members collectively procure yarn and handle marketing, earning fair prices. The Tawa Matsya Sangh is a federation of fisherworker cooperatives fighting for displaced forest dwellers rights.
